title: Who should pick who gets the drug?
hook: Forty patients, one drug, twenty doses. Does it matter who decides who gets one?

doesNotKnow: that letting a person choose who is treated builds their judgement into the result, and that a coin breaks that link

misconception: A careful doctor who knows the patients assigns treatment as fairly as a coin flip; with 20 per group it evens out.
objective: The learner can explain that when a person chooses who is treated, whatever guides the choice (here fitness) shows up as a treatment effect, and that random assignment spreads it evenly over both groups.

claims.text: In the model (recovery chances evenly spaced from 30% to 90%), giving the drug to the 20 fittest makes expected recoveries 15.1 vs 8.9 of 20 with a drug that does nothing; she picked the fittest, so fitness passes for a cure.
claims.source: Arithmetic: chance_i = 30% + 60% i/39; top 20 mean 75.4%, bottom 20 mean 44.6% (gap 30.8 points); 20 x 0.754 = 15.1, 20 x 0.446 = 8.9. Brief 58 check (company/domains/briefs/checks/probability-round4-check.mjs); model.ts result(doctorSplit()).
claims.note: Derivation re-run in node (own copy of model.ts): the top 20 sum to 15.077 and the bottom 20 to 8.923 expected recoveries, shown as 15.1 vs 8.9, gap +6.2 (= 30.8 points x 20/100). The switch to expected recoveries is consistent: the boxes, the gap line and the reveal all use recoveries, and nothing on the stage says points.

claims.text: Under random assignment fit and frail patients land on both sides about equally: the expected gap is 0, with a standard deviation of about 5.7 points (about 1.1 recoveries). The card's coin splits use mulberry32(58), (59), ... in order: the first gives 11.8 vs 12.2 expected recoveries (gap −0.4), and the first 21 (the QA path: Coin picks, then +20 coins) give gaps from −2.0 to +1.6 recoveries, none near the doctor's +6.2.
claims.source: Variance of a difference of means under sampling without replacement: 2 sigma / sqrt(39), sigma = 17.75 points -> 5.69 (brief 58 check). Coin values: model.ts coinSplit(k) = Fisher-Yates shuffle with mulberry32(58 + k), first 20 get the drug; seeds 58, 59, ... in order, not chosen for their result. Builder's node re-run 2026-10-14 (kit mulberry32 copy): k = 0..20 gaps -0.4, -0.4, 0, -0.6, -0.2, +1.6, -0.6, -0.8, -1.2, +1.0, -2.0, -0.6, -0.4, -0.8, 0, -1.0, 0, -0.6, 0, -0.2, -1.0 (gap = difference of the 1-decimal box values).
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-821, 2026-10-14): coin presses now step through seeds and keep a tally of gaps; text now names the tallied range; previously verified by fact-checker on 2026-10-14. Earlier note: Derivation: sigma = 17.759 points, SD of the gap = 2 sigma / sqrt(39) = 5.69 points (own 200,000-split simulation: 5.69), which is 1.14 recoveries in the stage's unit. Coin splits from the kit mulberry32 (it matches the check script's generator over 1,000 draws): seed 58 gives 11.846 vs 12.154 and seed 59 gives 11.815 vs 12.185, both 11.8 vs 12.2. Non-blocking: the text gives the SD in points; 'about 1.1 recoveries' would match the stage. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Own node re-implementation (Fisher-Yates with mulberry32(58 + k), first 20 get the drug, gap = difference of 1-decimal box values): k = 0 gives 11.8 vs 12.2 (gap -0.4); k = 0..20 gaps -0.4, -0.4, 0, -0.6, -0.2, +1.6, -0.6, -0.8, -1.2, +1.0, -2.0, -0.6, -0.4, -0.8, 0, -1.0, 0, -0.6, 0, -0.2, -1.0: range -2.0 to +1.6. Doctor split 15.1 vs 8.9 (+6.2). SD of the gap: 2 sigma_pop / sqrt(39) = 5.69 points (my 200,000-split simulation: 5.69), = 1.14 recoveries. The new tally line and reveal range text are computed from these gaps.

claims.text: A gap as big as the doctor's turns up by coin less than 1 time in 100.
claims.source: Brief 58 check: mulberry32(58), 100,000 coin splits, |gap| >= 15 points in 0.74%; the doctor's gap (30.8 points) is larger still, about 5.4 standard deviations. Builder's cross-check with model.ts's shuffle, seeds 1058-101057: 0.72% at >= 15 points.
claims.note: Simulation re-run with my own seed, mulberry32(12345), 200,000 splits: a gap of 15 points or more came up in 0.72%, and a gap as big as the doctor's (30.8 points, 6.2 recoveries, z = 5.4) came up 0 times. So 'less than 1 time in 100' is true and understates the rarity. Non-blocking: the source quotes the 15-point rate, which is half the doctor's gap.

claims.text: The patients and the drug are a model, not data; in this model the drug does nothing.
claims.source: Lesson rule (brief 58 planned claim 4); stated on the stage caption 'In this model the drug does nothing.'
claims.note: Convention, consistent: the caption 'In this model the drug does nothing.' is on the stage, and result() adds chances only, with no drug term.

recall.question: A school lets teachers choose which pupils try a new reading app. App users score higher. Why is that weak evidence for the app?
options: Whatever guided the teachers' choice could explain the higher scores
recall.why: When a person picks who is treated, their judgement (keen pupils, strong readers) rides along into the result. A coin breaks that link.
